job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Diego Walsh

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my parents on the family dairy farm outside Mallow, in County Cork. I'm up at six to help with the milking, then I shower and sit at the kitchen table to send applications. In the afternoon I update my portfolio, and in the evening I go to Mass with my mother on Sundays and to the pub quiz with my mates on Thursdays. I finished software engineering at University College Cork seven months ago.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What did you build in your final project, and where did you intern?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My final project was an inventory and breeding-record app for a local farm co-op, and it got a first. I did one internship at a farm machinery dealer's IT department and one at a small insurance software firm. I like building things that real people use. I've had five interviews and no offer yet, which my dad finds odd, since he thinks a good worker always gets hired.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that sounds about right. Every decade a new thing arrives, and the work carries on. I'd tell my mates at the pub quiz that a person who turns up and does the work properly will always be wanted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm a little uneasy. The farm is under pressure from milk prices and rules, and my dad is sixty. If I don't get a job, I'd be expected to help more at home, and I'm not sure I want a life in the milking parlour. A plateau means my future depends on the farm and the job market, and neither is easy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep applying in Cork city, where most software firms are. I'd ask the insurance firm's manager whether a role is coming up. I'd keep working on the co-op app, because two other co-ops asked about it. And I'd help my dad on weekends, but I wouldn't give up my job search.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alright, a bit heavy. It isn't fear, just the feeling that I'm in the middle of two worlds. I love the farm but it isn't my future.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did the machinery dealer's IT team do with new tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: How do you and your father talk about it?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does the farm shape your plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He says, you've a good degree, something will come. He means it kindly. I say yes, Dad, and don't tell him how many rejections I got. I want my father to see me earn a salary, not be an extra pair of hands.

say: I'd say it sounds about right: a new thing every decade, and the work **carries on**.
I'd tell mates a person who turns up and does the work **properly** will be wanted.
think: I'm a little **uneasy**: the farm is under pressure and my dad is sixty.
My future depends on the **farm** and the job market, and neither is easy.
do: Keep applying in **Cork city**, where most software firms are.
Ask the insurance firm's manager whether a **role** is coming up.
Keep building the **co-op app**, since two other co-ops asked about it.
feel: A bit **heavy**, in the middle of two worlds.
S0.quote: I want my father to see me earn a salary, not be an extra pair of hands.
fieldNote: His unease comes from the **farm's** money pressure and family expectations, not from AI.
He hides rejections from his father, showing a gap between the public and private line.
The co-op app is a live asset he can use.

steps.text: Apply to Cork city software firms every weekday
Ask the insurance firm manager about upcoming graduate posts
Offer the co-op app to the two other co-ops that asked

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's no use panicking. People should learn the tools and keep their trade. I'd say firms should train young people, and families should help them through. I wouldn't blame anyone, I'd just say work harder and adapt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be uneasy. Tests, small fixes and documentation are the things I'd do in my first year, and the tools do those fast. I'd worry that Cork firms will hire a few seniors with AI rather than a few juniors. But I have a skill that firms could use: I understand farm software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use an AI assistant now and then to speed up my own work, and I'd keep a close eye on what it produces. I'd aim for agri-tech firms, because they need people who know farming and code. I'd also build more of the co-op app, as a way to show real skills. And if nothing came, I'd help my dad for a year while I applied.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but steady. It's like a wet spring, where the fields are slow but you keep going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which parts of a junior developer's job would the software take?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The farm is a cushion and a pull. If the job market dries up, I could always go home, and that's some comfort. But I'd also be stuck, with dad's farm to run in a world where small farms struggle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does that mean for the farm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The thinking tasks, like tests and docs, go first. The part where I talk to a farmer and work out what the farm needs is the part the tools don't do.

say: I'd say there's no use panicking: people should learn the tools and keep their **trade**.
I'd say firms should **train** young people.
think: Tests, small fixes and documentation are my first-year tasks, and the tools do them **fast**.
I understand **farm software**, which firms could use.
do: Use an AI assistant now and then and **check** its output.
Aim for **agri-tech** firms that need people who know farming and code.
Help my dad for a **year** if nothing comes.
feel: **Uneasy** but steady, like a wet spring: slow, but you keep going.
S1.quote: The part where I talk to a farmer and work out what the farm needs is the part the tools don't do.
fieldNote: He sees farm knowledge as a **niche** that sets him apart.
The farm acts as both **cushion** and trap, and he knows it.
He stays steady, matching his moderate openness.

steps.text: Use an AI assistant on my co-op app and review each change
Apply to agri-tech software firms in Cork and Limerick
Help my dad on the farm for a year if no offer comes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've to look after each other. Families, parishes and local groups will matter more than governments. I'd say the state should help, but I'd say it's work and community that keep people going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm anxious. The thinking side of my work would be done by machines, and I'd have no track record. The farm would be hit too, since robots may milk cows and drive tractors from around 2031, and dairy prices would tumble if everyone uses them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take any job I can get, even outside software, and I'd start paying my way at home. I'd save everything, and I'd learn the machine side of dairy, like robotic milking systems, since farms will need people who can fix them. I'd also try a part-time course in mechatronics. And I'd lean on the parish and the local co-op, who know me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, with a stone in the stomach. I'd feel I should have started earlier, and I'd probably say a prayer or two. But I'd also feel I'm not alone, and that's some comfort.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years. What happens to the farm, and to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My faith says to do your best and trust the rest. That doesn't pay the bills, but it helps me sleep. I'd also trust my mother's judgement, because she has lived through harder times, like the cattle price crash.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where do your beliefs come in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk with my dad about whether the farm can survive. He'd hate it, and I'd feel awful for raising it. But I'd rather have an honest talk in November than a sad one in five years.

say: I'd say we've to **look after each other**, and parishes and local groups will matter.
I'd say work and **community** keep people going.
think: The thinking side of my work goes to machines and I'd have **no track record**.
Robots on the farm from 2031 could tumble dairy **prices**.
do: Take any job I can get, even outside **software**.
Learn the machine side of dairy, like **robotic milking** systems.
Lean on the **parish** and the local co-op.
feel: **Anxious**, with a stone in the stomach, but not alone.
S2.quote: I'd rather have an honest talk in November than a sad one in five years.
fieldNote: He turns to **community** and faith, which fits his traditional outlook.
His strongest worry covers the **farm's** future, not only his own job.
He plans a pivot toward dairy machine servicing.

steps.text: Take any paid job I can get in Cork, even outside software
Take a part-time mechatronics course for dairy machine repair
Save every euro of pay and pay board to my parents
Talk to the parish and the co-op about local work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a fair length, and people should use it. I'd tell the lads to learn a trade or something they can do with their hands, and to keep their savings in order. I'd keep it practical.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be uneasy but hopeful. I could get a software job, spend three or four years in it, then move into agri-tech or farm technology. That's a path I could see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the best software job I can find, save, and keep up with the AI tools as they come. I'd also help my dad invest in a robotic milker, if the numbers work, because it would cut his workload. And I'd learn more about farm finances, so I'm useful to the family and not just on screens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mixed, mostly steady. It feels like the weather forecast is bad but not terrible, so you move the cattle and keep going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would five years give you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work on it part-time, probably, in some form. I'd love to keep the land in the family, but not at the cost of my own life. Perhaps I'd run the technology side while someone else milks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still want to work on the farm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives time to plan the handover between my dad and me. If we start now, it can be gentle. If it's rushed, it becomes a fight, and I've seen that on other farms.

say: I'd say five years is a fair length and people should **use it**.
I'd tell the lads to learn something they can do with their **hands**.
think: I'd be uneasy but **hopeful**: a software job then agri-tech is a path I can see.
I'd love to keep the **land** in the family, but not at the cost of my life.
do: Take the best **software job** and keep up with AI tools.
Help my dad look at a **robotic milker** if the numbers work.
Learn farm **finances** so I'm useful to the family.
feel: **Steady**, like a forecast that's bad but not terrible.
S3.quote: I'd love to keep the land in the family, but not at the cost of my own life.
fieldNote: The longer horizon lets him think about the **handover** between him and his father.
He pairs a software career with **farm technology**.
Pressure remains, so anxious, not calm.

steps.text: Take the best software job offered in Cork
Price a robotic milker with my dad and the bank
Use AI tools at work and learn new ones as they come
Plan a gentle farm handover with my dad over five years

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, and we'll adapt, as we always do. I'd tell friends to work, marry, and save, and not to waste the time. I'd be calm in public.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm calm, mostly. By 33 I could be married, in a good job, with a small piece of land. The tools will change, but families and farms still need people who turn up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work in software for a few years, then perhaps bring those skills home to run the farm's systems. I'd save for a house, probably on the farm's edge. I'd learn each tool as it arrives, but I'd not rush into every one. And I'd keep going to Mass and the community events, because that's where my friends and my future wife may be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Settled, I'd say. Not thrilled, but at peace. It feels like looking forward to harvest after a long summer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, what does your life look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them that work matters, that family matters, and that a person who adapts doesn't have to lose who they are. That's what my grandad did when he went from horses to tractors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want your own children to know?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd also say that land is more than money. Even if machines do the work, there's something in knowing where you come from. I'd want them to feel that, even if the farm is smaller by then.

say: I'd say ten years is a long time and **we'll adapt**, as we always do.
I'd tell friends to work, marry and **save**.
think: I'm mostly **calm**: by 33 I could be married with a good job.
Families and farms still need people who **turn up**.
do: Work in software for a few years, then bring skills home to the **farm**.
Save for a **house** on the farm's edge.
Learn each tool as it arrives, but not **rush**.
feel: **Settled**, like looking forward to harvest after a long summer.
S4.quote: A person who adapts doesn't have to lose who they are. That's what my grandad did when he went from horses to tractors.
fieldNote: Time lets him link **tradition** and change: family, faith and land.
His calm is real but a thread of **unease** stays about the farm's future.
He uses his grandfather's story as a model.

steps.text: Work in software for three years, then bring skills to the farm
Save a deposit for a house on the farm's edge
Plan to marry and settle near Mallow by 28
Keep going to Mass and the community events

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one worries me most. It would hit my work and the farm at the same time, with no time to adjust. What would help is jobs that fit graduates, support for family farms, and people in the parish looking out for each other.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: It's not only about my job. My dad's whole life is that farm, and the thought that it might not make sense for me is the heaviest part. I'd like people to know that the farm is part of every answer I gave.

headlineQuote: My dad's whole life is that farm, and the thought that it might not make sense for me is the heaviest part.
portrait: Diego is **23**, a software engineering graduate from County Cork, living on his family's dairy farm.
He uses AI tools now and then and treats them as **useful but second** to hard work.
His worries are shaped by the **farm** and his father, as much as by his own job.
He trusts family, faith and community, and plans to bring his **software skills** home.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** AGI picture, which would hit his career and the farm together.
whatWouldHelp: Jobs that fit **graduates**, support for family farms and a parish that looks out for each other.
